q: What is the primary purpose of the scope document and rules of engagement in a penetration test?
opts: Administrative paperwork required by the client
Your legal protection as a tester
A technical checklist of tools to use
A marketing document for the client
exp: The scope and rules of engagement define what you are authorised to test and how. Without them, any access to a target system could constitute an offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990.

q: What is the main benefit of following a repeatable penetration testing lifecycle?
opts: It makes the report look professional
It allows you to charge more for each engagement
It keeps the methodology consistent and defensible across any organisation
It reduces the number of tools you need to use
exp: A repeatable lifecycle ensures consistency - every engagement follows the same structured phases regardless of client, so findings are comparable and the methodology can be defended.

q: Under the Computer Misuse Act 1990, what is the maximum penalty for the Section 1 offence of unauthorised access to computer material?
exp: Section 1 covers basic unauthorised access. Maximum sentence is 2 years. This is the baseline offence - even using someone else's credentials without permission qualifies.

q: Which section of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 covers unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate further offences?
exp: Section 2 elevates the offence when the attacker intends to use that access to commit a further crime such as fraud or blackmail. Maximum sentence is 5 years.

q: Which UK Act was introduced in 2015 and added Section 3ZA to the Computer Misuse Act, covering acts causing serious damage?
exp: The Serious Crime Act 2015 added Section 3ZA to the CMA, specifically to address attacks on critical national infrastructure such as power grids, water systems, and hospitals. Maximum sentence is life imprisonment.

q: What does CVSS stand for, and what is it used for in penetration testing?
opts: Common Vulnerability Severity Score - rates the difficulty of exploitation
Common Vulnerability Scoring System - a universally recognised way to score vulnerability severity
Cyber Vulnerability Security Standard - a UK government framework
Critical Vulnerability Scanning System - an automated scanning tool
Certified Vulnerability Summary Sheet - a reporting template
exp: CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) provides a standardised, vendor-neutral score from 0 to 10. A score of 9.1 means the same thing to any client anywhere in the world.

q: Why is CVSS important to use when reporting vulnerability severity to a client?
opts: It is required by GDPR for all security assessments
It automatically patches vulnerabilities once scored
It is universally recognised, so the score means the same thing to any client anywhere in the world
It is the only scoring system accepted by CREST
It eliminates the need to write an explanation
exp: CVSS is a universal language for severity. Without it, 'quite serious' or 'high risk' means different things to different people. A CVSS score is consistent and internationally understood.

q: What ICMP type does the ping command send as an echo request?
exp: ICMP Type 8 is the Echo Request - what ping sends. ICMP Type 0 is the Echo Reply. Type 8 is the question, Type 0 is the answer.

q: In Nmap, what does the -sn flag do?
opts: Performs a stealth SYN scan on all ports
Performs a ping scan (host discovery only, no port scanning)
Scans for service versions on open ports
Runs all default NSE scripts against a target
exp: -sn tells Nmap to discover which hosts are alive without scanning ports. Use it first on a large subnet to build a list of live targets before running a full port scan.

q: In Nmap, what does the -PE flag tell Nmap to use as its host discovery probe?
exp: -PE tells Nmap to send ICMP echo requests (pings) for host discovery. Combined with -sn it performs classic ping-based host discovery.

q: In Nmap, what does the -sS flag perform?
exp: -sS is the SYN scan. It sends a SYN, receives a SYN/ACK, then sends a RST - never completing the handshake. Faster and stealthier than a full connect scan (-sT).

q: In Nmap, what does the -sC flag do?
opts: Runs the default set of Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) scripts
Counts the number of open ports found
exp: -sC runs Nmap's default NSE scripts. These are categorised as safe and enumerate additional service information without actively exploiting anything.

q: What is ARP, and why is it useful in network reconnaissance?
opts: Address Resolution Protocol - maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local network
Automated Recon Protocol - a hacking tool for scanning hosts
Advanced Routing Protocol - used to find network routes
Application Response Protocol - measures server response times
Address Routing Protocol - maps hostnames to MAC addresses
exp: ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses at Layer 2. The ARP cache on a machine shows which hosts it has recently communicated with - passive local recon without sending any network probes.

q: What is Wireshark used for in network reconnaissance?
opts: Scanning open ports on remote hosts
Capturing and analysing network traffic packets
exp: Wireshark is a packet capture and analysis tool. It lets you inspect network traffic in real time and review captures offline. Essential for understanding what is on the wire.

q: What is the key difference between passive and active reconnaissance?
opts: Passive recon uses commercial tools; active recon uses free tools
Passive recon gathers information without directly interacting with the target; active recon involves direct interaction
Passive recon is illegal without authorisation; active recon is always legal
Passive recon only works on internal networks; active recon works on the internet
Passive recon uses OSINT; active recon uses social engineering
exp: Passive recon (Shodan, DNS lookups, GitHub) sends no traffic to the target. Active recon (Nmap scans, banner grabbing) interacts directly with the target and can be detected.

q: What is banner grabbing?
opts: Capturing screenshots of a target web application
Connecting to a service on an open port to read the information it advertises about itself
Downloading the HTTP headers from a web server
Cloning a website for credential harvesting
exp: Banner grabbing connects to an open port and reads what the service responds with - software name, version, OS details. Services often reveal more than they should in their banners.

q: What service runs on TCP port 21?
exp: Port 21 is FTP's control channel. Port 20 is the data channel. FTP transmits credentials in plaintext. Anonymous FTP (no credentials required) is an immediate finding.

q: What service typically runs on TCP port 22?
exp: Port 22 is SSH - Secure Shell. Encrypted remote access. The correct replacement for Telnet. Look for weak credentials, old versions, and misconfigured key-based auth.

q: What service runs on TCP port 80?
exp: Port 80 is HTTP - unencrypted web traffic. Everything is plaintext. If a site runs only on 80 with no 443 redirect, that is a finding.

q: What service runs on TCP port 443?
exp: Port 443 is HTTPS - HTTP encrypted with TLS. The standard for all modern web traffic.

q: What service runs on TCP port 445, and what is it used for?
opts: RDP - Remote Desktop Protocol for graphical remote access
DNS - Domain Name Service for name resolution
SMB - Server Message Block, used to share files and printers across Microsoft networks
NFS - Network File Share used in Unix environments
exp: Port 445 is SMB - Microsoft file and printer sharing. Always a priority target. Associated with EternalBlue and WannaCry. Finding 445 open demands investigation.

q: What is SMB, and what notorious malware exploited a vulnerability in it?
opts: Simple Mail Block - exploited by Mirai
Server Message Block - exploited by WannaCry
Secure Message Broker - exploited by NotPetya
System Management Bus - exploited by Stuxnet
Standard Messaging Base - exploited by Conficker
exp: SMB (Server Message Block) is Microsoft's file sharing protocol. WannaCry in 2017 exploited EternalBlue, a vulnerability in SMBv1, to self-propagate across networks with no user interaction - infecting over 200,000 systems in 150 countries within 24 hours.

q: What service runs on UDP port 161?
exp: Port 161 UDP is SNMP - Simple Network Management Protocol. Used to monitor and manage network devices. Note: UDP not TCP. This comes up in the exam.

q: In SNMPv1, what are 'community strings'?
opts: Encrypted passwords used to authenticate network administrators
The equivalent of passwords used to authenticate access to SNMP - typically 'public' for read and 'private' for write
Network addresses used to group SNMP devices
Commands used to query SNMP-enabled devices
Certificate strings used to secure SNMP traffic
exp: SNMPv1 community strings are cleartext authentication tokens. 'public' is the default read-only string. 'private' is the default read-write string. If unchanged, an attacker can query and potentially configure any device.

q: What is the default SNMPv1 community string for read-only access to a device?
exp: The default read-only community string in SNMPv1 is 'public'. If a device has not had this changed, anyone who knows this can query it. Finding default community strings is a significant finding.

q: What is an SMB null session?
opts: A failed SMB connection caused by a misconfigured firewall
An SMB connection established without providing a username or password, historically allowed by Microsoft for network administration
An encrypted SMB session with no data transmitted
An SMB connection over an unencrypted Wi-Fi network
exp: An SMB null session is an anonymous connection to an SMB service - no username, no password. Historically permitted on Windows for browsing network shares. Finding null sessions enabled is a significant misconfiguration.

q: What does DNS stand for, and what does it do?
opts: Dynamic Network Service - assigns IP addresses automatically
Domain Name System - translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses
Distributed Network Scanning - a technique for mapping large networks
Data Network Standard - a protocol for transferring files
Dynamic Naming Service - resolves MAC addresses to hostnames
exp: DNS (Domain Name System) translates domain names like example.com into IP addresses. It runs on UDP port 53 for queries and TCP port 53 for zone transfers.

q: What does a /24 subnet mask mean in terms of available hosts?
opts: 254 usable host addresses (256 minus network and broadcast)
It depends on the IP class
exp: A /24 means 24 bits are the network portion. That leaves 8 bits for hosts: 2^8 = 256 addresses. Subtract the network address and broadcast address and you get 254 usable host addresses.

q: What does the Linux command 'ip a' show you?
opts: Active network connections to remote hosts
All running processes on the system
The network interface configuration including IP addresses
exp: 'ip a' (ip addr) shows all network interfaces and their IP addresses, MAC addresses, and state. The modern equivalent of ifconfig.

q: In the context of penetration testing, what should you always ask yourself about every technique and piece of information?
opts: How much would this cost to exploit commercially?
What would an attacker do with this information?
How quickly can this be automated?
Which CVSS score does this technique belong to?
Is this technique covered by the scope document?
exp: Every piece of information gathered during a test should be evaluated through an attacker's lens. This mindset drives prioritisation and helps you think beyond individual findings to chains of exploitation.

q: Using the driving analogy from Session 3, what does Module A (methodology/law) represent, and what does Module B (technical skills) represent?
opts: Module A is the engine; Module B is the highway code
Module A is the highway code (rules); Module B is sitting behind the wheel (how the engine works)
Module A is the MOT certificate; Module B is learning to drive
Module A is the road map; Module B is the destination
Module A is the fuel; Module B is the steering
exp: Module A is the highway code - the rules, the law, the professional framework. Module B is sitting behind the wheel - the technical skills you use on every test.

q: What are IoT devices and why are they particularly vulnerable from a security perspective?
opts: Internet of Things devices - they are vulnerable because they use strong encryption that is hard to audit
Internet of Things devices - they are frequently connected to public networks, rarely updated or patched, and may have no traditional user interface
Internal of Things devices - they are vulnerable because they use proprietary protocols
Internet of Tools devices - they are vulnerable because they expose APIs to the internet
Interconnected of Things devices - they are vulnerable due to Bluetooth weaknesses
exp: IoT devices (Internet of Things) are internet-connected physical devices - cameras, thermostats, industrial sensors. They are frequently shipped with default credentials, rarely patched, and often have no easy way to update firmware.

q: What is SCADA and where would you typically find it?
opts: Secure Cloud Architecture for Data Assets - found in banking systems
Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition - specialist industrial control systems found in power stations, water plants, railways, and factories
Security Compliance and Audit framework - found in government organisations
Scalable Computing and Data Analysis - found in data centres
Secure Communications and Data Aggregation - found in telecoms
exp: SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) systems monitor and control industrial processes. Finding SCADA systems on Shodan exposed to the internet is a critical finding - these control physical infrastructure.

q: What is Shodan, and how does a penetration tester use it?
opts: A port scanner similar to Nmap but designed for internal networks
A search engine that indexes internet-connected devices and their open ports and banners
A tool for capturing wireless network traffic
A tool for brute-forcing SSH credentials
exp: Shodan continuously scans the internet and indexes what it finds - open ports, service banners, software versions. Using Shodan is entirely passive - you query Shodan's database, sending nothing to the target.

q: Why can't you use Nmap to scan the IP address 192.168.0.2 from across the internet?
opts: Because Nmap doesn't support scanning IP addresses starting with 192
Because 192.168.0.2 is a private IP address and is not routable over the public internet
Because port scanning is illegal without a firewall exception
Because Nmap requires a VPN connection to scan any target
exp: 192.168.0.0/16 is a private range defined in RFC 1918. Private IPs are not routed over the public internet. You cannot reach them from outside the network they belong to without an internal foothold.

q: What is a significant security risk of developers using public GitHub repositories for their code?
opts: GitHub automatically publishes all commits to social media
GitHub limits file sizes, forcing developers to split sensitive data
Developers accidentally commit credentials, passwords, and API keys alongside their code, making them publicly accessible
GitHub does not support two-factor authentication
GitHub retains deleted files for only 24 hours
exp: Developers routinely accidentally commit API keys, database credentials, and passwords. Even after deletion, the commit history remains. GitHub recon before touching a target can yield credentials with zero interaction with the target.

q: In the context of GitHub recon, what does 'forking a repository' mean?
opts: Downloading all commits from a repository's history
Creating your own copy of someone else's repository to work on independently
Cloning a repository to your local machine
exp: Forking creates your own copy of a repository under your GitHub account. This is relevant in recon because forks preserve deleted content - if someone removed sensitive data from a repo, it may still exist in a fork.

q: A tester reviews public DNS records without contacting the target organisation. What type of reconnaissance is this?
exp: Reviewing public DNS records sends no traffic to the target. It is passive reconnaissance - gathering intelligence from public sources without the target being able to detect or log your activity.

q: What service runs on TCP port 23?
exp: Port 23 is Telnet - unencrypted remote access. Everything including passwords is transmitted in plaintext. Finding Telnet open in a modern environment is a significant finding. SSH (port 22) is the secure replacement.

q: What service runs on TCP port 25?
opts: SMTP - email routing between mail servers
exp: Port 25 is SMTP - Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. Used for routing email between mail servers. Can be used for user enumeration (VRFY/EXPN commands) on misconfigured servers.

q: What service runs on TCP port 110?
opts: POP3 - email retrieval to a single device
exp: Port 110 is POP3 - Post Office Protocol version 3. Downloads emails to a single device and deletes from the server. Unencrypted. The encrypted version is POP3S on port 995.

q: What service runs on TCP port 111?
opts: RPC/Portmapper - directory of RPC services on Unix/Linux
exp: Port 111 is RPC Portmapper on Unix/Linux systems. It acts as a directory - query it to find which other RPC-based services are running on the host. Useful for further enumeration.

q: What service runs on TCP port 135?
exp: Port 135 is MS-RPC - Microsoft Remote Procedure Call. The Windows equivalent of the Unix portmapper. Associated with many historical Windows vulnerabilities.

q: What service runs on TCP port 139?
opts: NetBIOS - legacy Microsoft name resolution and file sharing
exp: Port 139 is NetBIOS Session Service - legacy Microsoft file sharing and name resolution. Finding 139 and 445 together indicates an older Windows target. NetBIOS should not be exposed externally.

q: What service runs on TCP port 143?
opts: IMAP - email retrieval with multi-device sync
exp: Port 143 is IMAP - Internet Message Access Protocol. Unlike POP3 it syncs across multiple devices and keeps mail on the server. The encrypted version is IMAPS on port 993.

q: What service runs on TCP port 993?
exp: Port 993 is IMAPS - IMAP secured with SSL/TLS. The encrypted version of IMAP (port 143). If you find 143 open but not 993, that is a finding.

q: What service runs on TCP port 995?
exp: Port 995 is POP3S - POP3 secured with SSL/TLS. The encrypted version of POP3 (port 110).

q: What service runs on TCP port 1723?
opts: PPTP - Point-to-Point Tunnelling Protocol, a legacy VPN protocol
exp: Port 1723 is PPTP - Point-to-Point Tunnelling Protocol. A legacy VPN protocol with known cryptographic weaknesses. Finding this indicates older VPN infrastructure.

q: What service runs on TCP port 2048?
exp: Port 2048 is NFS - Network File System. Linux/Unix file sharing, the equivalent of SMB for Unix systems. Misconfigured NFS exports can expose significant portions of a filesystem.

q: What service runs on TCP port 3306?
exp: Port 3306 is MySQL. Database servers should never be directly internet-facing. Finding MySQL open externally is a critical finding - immediate investigation required.

q: What service runs on TCP port 3389?
opts: RDP - Remote Desktop Protocol for graphical Windows remote access
exp: Port 3389 is RDP - Remote Desktop Protocol. Graphical remote access to Windows systems. High-value target for credential attacks. BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) was an RDP vulnerability with a CVSS of 9.8.

q: What service typically runs on TCP port 8080?
opts: HTTP alternate - dev servers, proxies, and admin panels
exp: Port 8080 is an alternative HTTP port. Used for development servers, proxy services, and admin panels. Worth investigating - admin interfaces on non-standard ports are often less hardened.

q: What is the correct port number for DNS?
exp: DNS runs on port 53. UDP for standard queries, TCP for zone transfers. Zone transfer misconfiguration (AXFR) can expose a full map of every hostname in a domain.

q: An Nmap scan returns port 445/tcp open. What service does this indicate and what is the first thing you should investigate?
opts: RDP is open - check for BlueKeep
HTTP is open - check the web application
SMB is open - check for EternalBlue and null sessions
DNS is open - attempt a zone transfer
FTP is open - try anonymous login
exp: Port 445 is SMB. When you find it open, immediately check the SMB version (is SMBv1 enabled?), check for EternalBlue vulnerability, and attempt null session enumeration.

q: What is the port pairing for POP3 and its encrypted equivalent?
exp: POP3 runs on port 110. POP3S (POP3 over SSL/TLS) runs on port 995. If you find 110 open but not 995, unencrypted email retrieval is a finding.

q: What is the port pairing for IMAP and its encrypted equivalent?
exp: IMAP runs on port 143. IMAPS (IMAP over SSL/TLS) runs on port 993. Finding 143 open without 993 means email is being retrieved unencrypted.

q: An Nmap scan shows port 23/tcp open on a server. What is the significance of this finding?
opts: The server is running a secure remote access service
The server is running Telnet - all traffic including credentials is transmitted in plaintext
The server is running SMTP and may relay email
The server is running an alternate web service
The server is running a legacy FTP service
exp: Port 23 is Telnet. Finding it open means any administrator logging in remotely is transmitting their username and password in plaintext, visible to anyone on the same network segment.

q: Which of the following ports would you expect to find open on a Windows server used for remote administration?
exp: Port 3389 is RDP - Remote Desktop Protocol - used for graphical remote administration of Windows servers. Finding it open externally with no IP restrictions is a significant finding.
